title: Quantitative effects of head rotation angle on apnea hypopnea index in positional obstructive sleep apnea – a preliminary case series

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec> <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title> <jats:p>Quantify the effects of head rotation and head incline on obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity.</jats:p> </jats:sec><jats:sec> <jats:title>Design</jats:title> <jats:p>Single-arm, intervention study.</jats:p> </jats:sec><jats:sec> <jats:title>Setting</jats:title> <jats:p>Pulmonary specialty clinic.</jats:p> </jats:sec><jats:sec> <jats:title>Case presentation</jats:title> <jats:p>Ten adults diagnosed with positional OSA ranging from 32 to 64 years of age 6 females, 4 males reporting persistent daytime sleepiness and health issues with consistent use of CPAP.</jats:p> </jats:sec><jats:sec> <jats:title>Intervention</jats:title> <jats:p>Standard polysomnography with a head angle sensor attached to the forehead and coaching to fall asleep with head at various rotation and incline angles and torso in supine and non-supine positions.</jats:p> </jats:sec><jats:sec> <jats:title>Measurements</jats:title> <jats:p>OSA severity was scored according to American Academy of Sleep Medicine guidelines. Apnea hypopnea index (AHI) and peripheral capillary oxygen (SpO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>) saturation were measured during each sleep epoch of unique head rotation, head incline, and torso position.</jats:p> </jats:sec><jats:sec> <jats:title>Results</jats:title> <jats:p>Two participants (1 with no apneas and 1 with central sleep apnea) were excluded. Among the remaining 8 participants, average reduction in peak AHI was 66% (range 18–88%) with head rotation ≤ 20° above the horizon compared with > 20° above the horizon. The average of peak AHI values with head rotation ≤ 20° was significantly lower than with head rotation > 20° (20.0 vs 45.3, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.002). Minimum SpO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> was significantly higher for head rotation ≤ 20° compared with > 20° (mean: 90.6% vs 84.3%, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.03). In the torso supine position, average peak AHI was significantly lower with head rotation ≤ 20° compared with > 20° (7.1 vs 52.1, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.001). In the torso non-supine position, lower average peak AHI with head rotation ≤ 20° was not statistically significant (22.3 vs 38.4, <jats:italic>P</jats:italic> = 0.09).</jats:p> </jats:sec><jats:sec> <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title> <jats:p>These results support further exploration of maintaining head position ≤ 20° above the horizon to minimize AHI and oxygen desaturation in OSA patients.</jats:p> </jats:sec><jats:sec> <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title> <jats:p>Apnea Hypopnea Index Severity Versus Head Position During Sleep.</jats:p> <jats:p>ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04086407 September 11, 2019 Registered retrospectively.</jats:p> </jats:sec>
